To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“A chemical carcinogen is a compound that causes cancer by interacting with DNA, either directly or after metabolic activation, to induce mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle, and that these mutations can lead to the formation of a malignant tumor.

1) the chemical carcinogen benzo(a)pyrene is metabolized in the liver of mice by a cytochrome P-450 enzyme, Cyp1a1, to an ultimate carcinogen, benzo(a)phenyl-2-ol; 2) this metabolite is detoxified by an enzyme, glutathione S-transferase, in the liver of rats; 3) the enzyme is inducible by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and

the carcinogenicity of a chemical can be assessed from the extent of its binding to DNA, that the carcinogenic potency of a chemical depends on its rate of metabolism to a DNA-reactive species, that the rate of metabolism of a chemical depends in turn on its chemical structure and the nature of the enzyme systems that metabolize it, and that the carcinogenic activity of a chemical depends, at least in part, on its ability to induce mutations in the DNA of target cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1. What are the causes of cancer in man? 2. How are these causes identified? 3. How are these identified causes prevented?
the detection of cancer hazards and the elucidation of mechanisms of carcinogenesis.

the identification and elucidation of the mechanisms of action of chemical carcinogens and the development of new approaches for the detection and evaluation of the carcinogenic hazards that may be presented to man in his environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the carcinogenic hazards of tobacco smoking have been demonstrated by a large number of epidemiological studies and that the evidence is overwhelming.

(1) the evidence for an association between exposure to asbestos and the subsequent development of cancer is strong; (2) the evidence for the association between exposure to tobacco smoke and the development of cancer in man is overwhelming; (3) the evidence for association between the use of oral contraceptives and cancer in women is strong; (4) the evidence for a relationship between the use of oestrogens in menopausal women and cancer of the breast is strong;
there is no convincing evidence to support a relationship between the consumption of alcohol and breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to identify the major carcinogens in the environment and have shown how they act to cause cancer.
we have made progress, but we are far from having a clear picture of how to proceed in the future.
the identification of carcinogens has been a major success story in toxicology, and that the identification of cancer hazards is a major challenge for the 1980s.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk of developing cancer is a complex interplay between the genetic makeup of an individual and their exposure to carcinogenic factors in the environment.
the cancer risk is higher in the first 10 years of life than in the rest of life combined.
the risk of developing cancer is a function of the dose of carcinogens to which a person is exposed and that the risk can be greatly reduced by reducing exposure to these carcinogens.
